Name: Step Pyramid of Djoser
Description: Designed by the royal vizier and architect Imhotep, this six-tiered monument is Egypt's earliest colossal stone building and the world's oldest surviving cut-stone pyramid. Evolving from a traditional flat-roofed mastaba tomb, it stands at the center of an expansive walled limestone funerary courtyard complex.

Name: Meidum Pyramid
Description: Originally built as a seven-stepped pyramid and expanded to eight steps before being encased in smooth limestone to form a true pyramid. Partial outer casing collapses in antiquity left its distinctive tower-like three-tiered core standing high above a massive collar of limestone rubble.

Name: Bent Pyramid
Description: A pivotal transitional monument in pyramid engineering whose lower walls rise at a steep 54-degree angle before shifting halfway up to a shallower 43-degree slope to prevent structural instability. It retains a greater proportion of its original polished outer Tura limestone casing than almost any other Egyptian pyramid.

Name: Red Pyramid (North Pyramid)
Description: The world's first successful true smooth-sided pyramid and the third-largest Egyptian pyramid after those of Khufu and Khafre at Giza. Named for the rusty reddish hue of its exposed iron-rich local limestone core blocks, its interior houses three towering corbel-vaulted chambers.

Name: Great Pyramid of Giza (Pyramid of Khufu)
Description: The largest and tallest pyramid ever constructed in Egypt, originally rising to 146.6 meters and assembled from roughly 2.3 million limestone and granite blocks. As the oldest and sole surviving monument of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World, it is celebrated for its precision engineering, Grand Gallery, and granite King's Chamber.

Name: Pyramid of Djedefre
Description: Erected atop a commanding natural promontory eight kilometers north of Giza, giving its foundation the highest elevation of any Old Kingdom pyramid. Extensively quarried for stone from the Roman period onward, its ruins still feature a dramatic open descending trench leading into a large subterranean burial pit.

Name: Pyramid of Khafre
Description: The second-largest pyramid at Giza, visually appearing taller than Khufu's neighboring monument because it sits on higher bedrock and rises at a slightly steeper angle. It retains a prominent cap of original smooth Tura limestone casing near its apex and connects via a monumental stone causeway to the Valley Temple and the Great Sphinx.

Name: Pyramid of Menkaure
Description: The smallest of the three primary Giza pyramids, originally standing around 65 meters high and distinguished by having its lowest sixteen courses encased in costly red Aswan granite rather than white limestone. Three smaller subsidiary queens' pyramids stand aligned beside its southern flank.

Name: Pyramid of Userkaf
Description: Built immediately northeast of Djoser's Step Pyramid enclosure, this monument heralded a shift toward smaller rubble-core pyramids paired with richly decorated temple complexes. Breaking with established canon, its main mortuary temple was placed along the southern side of the pyramid rather than the eastern face.

Name: Pyramid of Sahure
Description: The founding monument of the Abusir royal necropolis, establishing the standard architectural layout for Fifth and Sixth Dynasty funerary complexes. Though its stepped limestone core is heavily eroded, its mortuary temple and causeway are renowned for intricate wall reliefs, monolithic palmiform granite columns, and a copper-lined drainage system.

Name: Pyramid of Neferirkare Kakai
Description: The tallest and largest pyramid erected at Abusir, originally begun as a six-tiered step pyramid before being enlarged and converted into a true smooth-sided monument. Excavations in its mudbrick-completed mortuary temple uncovered the famous Abusir Papyri, providing detailed administrative records of Old Kingdom royal cults.

Name: Pyramid of Nyuserre Ini
Description: Positioned tightly between the complexes of Sahure and Neferirkare, Nyuserre's monument diverted and repurposed his father Neferirkare's unfinished causeway and valley temple. It features a distinctive L-shaped mortuary temple and stands south of Nyuserre's well-preserved sun temple at Abu Ghurab.

Name: Pyramid of Unas
Description: Modest in outward scale and eroded to a rounded mound, its underground chambers hold extraordinary historical importance as the first royal tomb inscribed with the Pyramid Texts. Hundreds of blue-pigmented hieroglyphic spells cover its white limestone walls beneath a star-carved gabled ceiling to safeguard the king's rebirth.

Name: Pyramid of Teti
Description: Located in North Saqqara, this pyramid's subterranean rooms continue the tradition of finely carved Pyramid Texts and house Egypt's earliest royal sarcophagus inscribed with funerary spells. Surrounding the monument is one of Saqqara's richest cemeteries of decorated mastabas belonging to Sixth Dynasty viziers and nobles.

Name: Pyramid of Pepi II
Description: The last major royal pyramid complex completed during the Old Kingdom, distinguished by an added masonry girdle wall reinforcing its base. Its underground chambers contain extensive Pyramid Texts, while three self-contained miniature pyramid complexes for his queens—Neith, Iput II, and Udjebten—flank the main monument.

Name: Pyramid of Senusret I
Description: One of the grandest pyramids of the Middle Kingdom, engineered around an internal framework of radiating limestone retaining walls filled with stone slabs and rubble beneath a smooth Tura limestone casing. Enclosed by two perimeter walls and nine smaller subsidiary pyramids, its temple yielded finely carved limestone statues of the pharaoh.

Name: Pyramid of Senusret II
Description: Constructed around a natural limestone knoll reinforced by stone cross-walls and millions of mudbricks, originally sheathed in polished white limestone. Breaking with centuries of tradition to deter tomb robbers, its entrance was hidden beneath a princess's tomb shaft on the southern side leading into a winding subterranean corridor.

Name: Black Pyramid (Pyramid of Amenemhat III)
Description: Named for its dark, weathered mudbrick core standing starkly against the desert landscape after its outer limestone casing was stripped away. Built on unstable clay ground too close to the Nile floodplain, its complex subterranean passages began cracking under its weight, prompting the king to construct a second pyramid at Hawara; its carved grey granite capstone survives in Cairo.

Name: Pyramid of Hawara
Description: Erected of mudbrick originally clad in white limestone as Amenemhat III's final burial monument, incorporating elaborate security measures such as blind passages, hidden ceiling trapdoors, and a monolithic quartzite burial chamber. Its vast adjoining mortuary temple was celebrated across the classical world by Herodotus and Strabo as the legendary 'Labyrinth.'

Name: Pyramid of Ahmose I
Description: Built as a royal cenotaph rather than a physical burial place, this monument represents the final royal pyramid constructed by a native pharaoh in Egypt before New Kingdom rulers shifted to rock-cut tombs in the Valley of the Kings. Formed from a sand-and-rubble core cased in fine limestone, it anchored a sprawling ceremonial complex honoring Ahmose and his grandmother Queen Tetisheri.
